item.title: 109 platoons of BGB deployed in Dhaka, five other districts
item.description:
A total of 109 platoons of Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) have been deployed in Dhaka and five other districts to maintain law and order, ensure public safety and prevent any untoward incidents.
Of the deployed platoons, 18 are in Savar and Ashulia of Dhaka, seven in Narayanganj, 18 in Gazipur, 56 in Gopalganj, three in Chittagong and seven in Cox's Bazar.
Another four platoons are on standby for deployment, BGB said in a press release on Friday morning.
Following directives from the Ministry of Home Affairs, BGB personnel are carrying out their duties in coordination with the respective district administration and other law enforcement agencies.
Apart from strengthening security and surveillance at key installations, industrial zones and other important locations, they are working to prevent disorder, violence and any activities that could threaten public safety.
Meanwhile, the BGB headquarters' monitoring cell is using modern technology to monitor and coordinate activities on the ground. The surveillance includes real-time monitoring of footage from drones, body-worn cameras and other advanced equipment.
Alongside their regular border duties, BGB personnel are also assisting in maintaining internal law and order, the force said.
The BGB reaffirmed its commitment to protecting public safety and property, ensuring the smooth movement of people and daily activities, and taking precautionary measures to deal with any unforeseen situation.

item.title: Eight Bangladeshis return home after two years in Indian jails
item.description:
Eight Bangladeshis have returned home after serving two-year prison sentences in India, where they had been arrested for entering the country illegally while seeking employment.
Indian immigration authorities facilitated their return by issuing special travel permits.
At around 8pm on Thursday, Indian immigration police at the Petrapole border handed them over to immigration police at the Benapole checkpost. Benapole Port Police later transferred them to the care of the NGO Justice and Care.
The returnees are from Faridpur, Chittagong, Narail, Jashore, Barguna, Panchagarh and Satkhira. According to police and NGO officials, they come from economically disadvantaged families and had crossed into India with the help of brokers in search of better livelihoods.
They found work in different sectors in Tamil Nadu and the Dum Dum area of Kolkata. However, police in Tamil Nadu and Dum Dum later arrested them on charges of illegal entry. A court sentenced them to two years in prison.
After completing their sentences, they were sent back to Bangladesh under special travel permits.
Saifur Rahman, officer-in-charge of Benapole Immigration Police, confirmed that the eight returnees had been handed over to Benapole Port Police after serving their prison terms in India.
Shafiqul Islam, a field worker for Justice and Care in Jashore, said the returnees would spend the night at the organisation's shelter home after being transferred from the port police station. They would subsequently be reunited with their families.

item.title: SC seeks explanation from ex-judge over primary teacher recruitment cases
item.description:
The Appellate Division has directed former High Court Division Justice Naima Haider to explain irregularities identified in the hearing and disposal of writ petitions concerning the recruitment of government primary school teachers.
The former judge, who has since resigned, has been asked to submit her explanation to the Registrar General of the Supreme Court by January 31.
The court has also barred two lawyers from practising before the Appellate Division and the High Court Division until further orders, pending an investigation into their conduct.
A five-member Appellate Division bench, led by Chief Justice Zubayer Rahman Chowdhury, passed the order on Thursday.
Justice Naima Haider resigned from the High Court Division on February 5, citing personal reasons, while the matter was under preliminary investigation by the Supreme Judicial Council.
In 2020, job seekers filed writ petitions alleging that the 60% quota for women in primary school teacher recruitment had not been properly implemented.
On August 9, 2023, a High Court bench headed by then-Justice Naima Haider delivered a verdict directing the appointment of the petitioners, provided they were found qualified based on their written and oral examination results.
Several other writ petitions concerning primary teacher recruitment were also filed, resulting in different judgments in 2023 and 2024. The government challenged the August 9, 2023 verdict and filed separate leave-to-appeal petitions in the other cases.
During hearings on the appeals and leave-to-appeal petitions, the government raised questions about irregularities in the handling of the writ petitions by the concerned High Court bench.
The Appellate Division summoned the relevant case files and, after examining 19 writ petitions, identified serious discrepancies in several cases. A committee headed by the Supreme Court Registrar General was subsequently formed to investigate the matter.
The committee submitted its report to the Appellate Division, which found serious discrepancies and irregularities in nine of the 19 cases.
The lawyers who appeared in those cases were Mohammad Siddiq Ullah Miah and Md Kamal Hossain.
In its order, the Appellate Division said the manner in which the concerned High Court bench allowed applications to add parties, bringing numerous individuals in as co-petitioners, appeared highly irregular.
The order referred to Writ Petition No. 15915, filed in 2023. The hearing concluded on April 28, 2024, but an order was issued on April 30 allowing another 574 individuals to be added as co-petitioners. The judgment was delivered on May 6.
However, the records showed that the names of the newly added co-petitioners were never included in the title of the writ petition, as required under the applicable rules. The judgment was delivered without the necessary amendment.
The Appellate Division described the manner in which the concerned bench conducted hearings and disposed of the rules as regrettable and inappropriate, adding that similar incidents had occurred in several other cases.
The Appellate Division directed the Bangladesh Bar Council to conduct a thorough investigation into the conduct of the two lawyers and submit a report to the Supreme Court Registrar General by January 31.
Pending the investigation, both lawyers have been barred from practising before the Appellate Division and the High Court Division.
The court also directed the Registrar General to immediately send a copy of the order and the investigation report to Justice Naima Haider and asked her to submit an explanation by January 31.
The matter has been scheduled for further orders on February 4.

item.title: Making plastic rules practical
item.description:
Adopting a European-style extended producer responsibility (EPR) framework to tackle plastic pollution is a welcome shift in policy ambition, moving the nation toward binding accountability for manufacturers, importers, and brand owners.
It was clear that merely relying primarily on government agencies and informal waste collectors was not sustainable nor fair. To that end, holding businesses accountable for the plastic they put on the market is the right way.
It goes without saying that plastic pollution continues to devastate our country. The result is choking canals, waterlogged streets, microplastics in food chains, and clogged drainage networks - all of which make aggressive action against plastic waste non-negotiable.
With that said, we agree with the concerns voiced by experts that importing a European regulatory model onto a very different economic landscape could fail unless the measures are grounded in feasibility, clear enforcement, and realistic local capacity.
The real test, as with any new policy or initiative, lies in practical execution rather than announcements. Shifting waste costs onto producers only reduces pollution if collection targets are verifiable, local sorting hubs exist, and companies cannot game the system through paper credits or unverified claims.
At the same time, slapping abrupt, uncalibrated compliance burdens onto smaller businesses or overlooking informal pickers and recyclers risks either driving activity underground or hurting livelihoods without cutting waste.
To make this framework work, the government must assist with practical infrastructure: Standardizing recyclable packaging, supporting local material recovery and recycling capacity, coordinating municipal waste collection, and integrating informal collectors into formal supply chains with fair protections are all steps that must be considered.
Tackling plastic pollution is essential for public health and urban resilience, especially in our major cities where the liveability deteriorates with every passing day. Practical, enforceable steps will determine whether the policy cleans up Bangladesh and helps us reduce the plastic burden.

item.title: Bangladesh needs more equity in healthcare
item.description:
A study by the Health Economics Unit (HEU) of the Ministry of Health has exposed something deeply disturbing in Bangladesh’s healthcare system: Wealthier citizens are increasingly claiming a larger share of benefits from public hospitals while poor families are being squeezed out.
Between 2016 and 2022, the share of public inpatient benefits going to the poorest two-fifths of households fell from 46% to 33%, whereas the wealthiest two-fifths saw their share rise from 28% to 38%.
When millions of ordinary Bangladeshis are already struggling under inflation, stagnant real wages, and economic strain, watching public healthcare fail those who need it most is simply unacceptable.
The financial fallout of this breakdown is devastating. Out-of-pocket medical expenses pushed over 1 crore Bangladeshis below the poverty line in 2022 - nearly double the 56 lakh impoverished by healthcare costs in 2005 - while over 90% of the poorest consumption group faced financial hardship from medical bills.
This is not what progress looks like for any nation, when low-income families are pushed into debt, asset sales, and prolonged illness.
Though the previous administration’s inability to address these issues or even identify how bad it was must be acknowledged, blaming past administrations alone cannot excuse ongoing inaction.
Metropolitan cities still lack accessible public primary and secondary facilities, pushing routine and emergency cases into crowded tertiary hospitals where connections and influence too often dictate access.
Government funding as a share of total health spending has also remained chronically low over the years. While the budget for health has increased this year, such an increase is meaningless if it does not reach those who need it most.
The Ministry of Health must work to restore genuine equity in public healthcare. Falling ill should never bankrupt the average citizen, and a more equitable nation is a better nation for all.

item.title: BGB files case over Gopalganj attack, names 5,008 accused
item.description:
Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) has filed a case over an attack on its patrol team in Tungipara, Gopalganj, in which government vehicles were torched, ammunition destroyed, and equipment looted.
Newton Molla, president of the banned Gopalganj District Chhatra League, has been named the prime accused. Seven others have also been named, while 5,000 unidentified people have been listed as accused, bringing the total number of accused to 5,008.
The named accused include Gopalganj District Chhatra League General Secretary Ataur Rahman Pial; former Tungipara upazila Chhatra League General Secretary Babul Hossain Khokon; current upazila Chhatra League President Shamshul Haque; Vice-President Ripon Sheikh; and Joint General Secretary Shahin Biswas, also known as Kalu.
The case was filed at Tungipara Police Station on November 23 following a complaint lodged by Nayeb Subedar Md Shawkat Ali of the BGB's Khulna Sector Headquarters.
Sakhawat Hossain Sentu, additional superintendent of police of Gopalganj's Sadar Circle, confirmed the matter on Thursday night.
According to the First Information Report (FIR), a BGB team was conducting patrols alongside police, Ansar personnel and Executive Magistrate Md Rihab Imam on November 17 to assist the civil administration in maintaining law and order in Gopalganj.
After receiving reports of vandalism and arson at Tungipara Police Station, the team headed towards the area. When they reached Nilfa Bazar in Tungipara, a group of people allegedly blocked the road by felling trees.
The FIR says the BGB personnel asked them to clear the road, but the group attacked them with improvised weapons and detonated crude bombs.
During the attack, a BGB armoured personnel carrier (APC) and a jeep were set on fire. Four BGB personnel — Nayek Md Monir Hossain, Asaduzzaman, Faruk Hossain and Assistant Director Md Saifiar Rahman — were seriously injured while attempting to intervene, according to the complaint.
The FIR states that a BGB Pajero jeep and an APC Cobra were completely destroyed by fire. Three submachine gun (SMG) magazines containing a total of 90 rounds of ammunition inside the jeep were also burnt.
The tyres and fog lights of another APC and the windshield of a pickup truck were damaged. A government-issued laptop, a walkie-talkie set, a battery and a charger kept inside the BGB vehicles were also allegedly looted.
The complaint estimates the total damage at Tk6.51 crore.
ASP Sentu said the case was filed over the attack, arson, vandalism and looting involving BGB personnel and vehicles. No arrests have been made so far, he added.

item.title: BNP leaders pay tribute to Dr Milon on his death anniversary
item.description:
Leaders of the Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) have paid tribute to Dr Shamsul Alam Khan Milon, who was killed during the anti-autocracy movement.
On Friday morning, BNP Acting Secretary General Ruhul Kabir Rizvi placed a wreath at Dr Milon's grave on the Dhaka Medical College premises.
He was accompanied by BNP Standing Committee member Professor Dr Farhad Halim Donar, the party's Health Affairs Secretary Dr Rafiqul Islam and leaders of the Doctors Association of Bangladesh (DAB).
The leaders stood in silence for a while, recited the Fatiha and offered prayers for the deceased. They also recalled Dr Milon's contributions and sacrifice during the 1990 anti-autocracy movement.
Meanwhile, student leaders who took part in the anti-autocracy movement organised a discussion at the National Press Club to commemorate Dr Milon.

item.title: What the ICJ’s landmark genocide finding could mean for the case against Israel in Gaza
item.description:
The International Court of Justice (ICJ) last week ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya minority group.
The court found Myanmar breached its obligations under the United Nations genocide convention to prevent and punish genocide.
This ruling is not just important for the Rohingya and Myanmar. It may also have a significant legal impact on other genocide cases before the court -- in particular, South Africa’s case alleging Israel has committed genocide in Gaza.
Other genocide cases
Four cases currently before the ICJ concern allegations of breaches of the genocide convention.
One was brought by Ukraine against Russia following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Another was brought by Nicaragua against Germany, regarding Germany’s support of Israel’s actions in Gaza. The third was brought by the Democratic Republic of Congo against Rwanda, which includes claims about Rwanda’s involvement in conflict in the Kivu provinces of the DRC.
The Myanmar ruling may have repercussions for all these cases.
However, the judgement will mostly affect the fourth genocide case before the court, the one brought by South Africa against Israel.
Multiple intents
Genocide is different from “ordinary” crimes in that it requires a “special intent” (or dolus specialis) -- the intent to destroy a national, racial, ethnic or religious group, in whole or in part.
This must be proven in addition to a general criminal intent, where a perpetrator intends to commit the crime or could have foreseen the result of their actions.
Genocidal intent is proven by two main forms of evidence. Firstly, there are the statements of political and military leaders, soldiers, the media and key figures in society. These often dehumanise the targeted group and may explicitly refer to the destruction of the group in some way.
The second way intent is proven is by looking at the perpetrators’ pattern of conduct.
In the Myanmar case, the court considered hate speech by Myanmar authorities against the Rohingya to be incitement to genocide. This formed evidence of intent.
The judges also used the military’s pattern of conduct to determine intent. Myanmar argued its intent was a counterinsurgency operation against a terrorist group, the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA). But the court determined the conduct of Myanmar’s security forces did not align with an intent to carry out a genuine counterinsurgency operation.
The court held that acts such killing civilians (including children), raping women, and destroying villages did not form part of legitimate military operations -- even if the operation also had the intent of meeting military objectives.
This is significant for the Israel genocide case because Israel argues it is fighting in self-defense in Gaza against a terrorist group, Hamas.
However, statements from Israeli government ministers about the intention to deny Palestinians necessities of life, or to erase Palestine from the map, may suggest a different intent.
As in the Myanmar case, the violence in Gaza has included the killing of civilians (including children), the widespread destruction of buildings (including in residential areas), and sexual and gender-based violence.
The Myanmar judgement gives the court an opening to decide that Israel has had both an intent to fight Hamas and a genocidal intent. Or it could decide Israel’s operations in Gaza do not represent a legitimate and lawful way to carry out an anti-terrorism military operation, which may demonstrate clear genocidal intent.
Killing of children
One of the key aspects of The Gambia’s case against Myanmar was that the killing of children demonstrated genocidal intent. The reason: Killing children is not a legitimate military objective.
The ICJ agreed. The court held that the killing of up to 2,000 children under the age of five was a significant indicator that Myanmar intended to destroy the future of the Rohingya people.
According to Gaza’s Ministry of Health, Israel has killed almost 22,000 children under 18 in Gaza. Some have been killed in indiscriminate attacks. Others have been deliberately targeted, according to the UN Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem, and Israel.
Following the court’s Myanmar decision, the killing of so many children in Gaza may strengthen the case against a legitimate military operation, and that the military and therefore the state instead had genocidal intent.
Broader context of crimes
The Myanmar case focused on the so-called “clearance operations” against the Rohingya in 2017. However, this violence was placed in the context of a lengthy history of discrimination and persecution of the Rohingya.
The court recognized that violations of human rights, which may not necessarily amount to genocidal crimes, were part of the bigger picture of the genocide. The exclusion of the Rohingya from citizenship was one example, as it denied them access to education, employment, healthcare, food and free movement.
Similarly, South Africa’s case against Israel positions the violence in Gaza since 2023 as an escalating step in decades of discrimination and persecution -- a system of apartheid -- against Palestinians.
Scale and targeting of crimes
ICJ judges also recognized that the scale of the crimes in Myanmar was relevant to the finding that genocide occurred, alongside the fact the violence specifically targeted the Rohingya. Thousands of Rohingya were killed and raped, and myriad Rohingya villages were destroyed. Non-Rohingya were not attacked, and their villages were not burned.
This has parallels to the situation in Gaza. Large numbers of Palestinians have been killed and injured, and huge swathes of Gaza have been destroyed.
It is estimated it will take many years and billions of dollars to clear and rebuild Gaza.
These findings have clear parallels with the situation in Gaza, and will undoubtedly be drawn on by South Africa as its case against Israel progresses in the coming years.
Melanie O'Brien is Professor of International Law, The University of Western Australia. This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license.

item.title: Trump downplays China and Russia's support to Iran
item.description:
US President Donald Trump on Thursday downplayed the importance of Russia and China's intelligence sharing with Iran, amid reports that Tehran's allies have helped it target US military bases.
Trump, during a short press conference with reporters at his Mar-a-Lago resort in Florida, noted that the Iran conflict had been discussed during his recent trilateral meeting with Chinese counterpart Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin.
"My meeting with President Xi was an incredible meeting. I think that they're very little involved with Iran. They could get involved, but involvement to me would mean shooting, not giving them little information," Trump said.
"We do the same thing, by the way. And you know, when they say that they may be spying on us, well, we spy on them too," he added.
Regarding Russia's intelligence sharing, Trump said: "I don't think they give very much."
He said both countries want to see the conflict with Iran end, and "I think they're helping me in that regard."
